extracted.intended_audience: scientists and academics who act as journal peer reviewers (including early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, disciplinary-agnostic guidance for crafting collegial, useful, and ethical peer-review reports for academic journals. Focuses on wording, tone, scope, ethics, and procedural best practices to increase constructiveness and reduce harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct comments at the work, not the authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer comments should evaluate the written manuscript and not attack or characterise the authors. Avoid ad hominem commentary (e.g. 'the authors completely failed to...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep criticism focused on sections of the manuscript (e.g. 'the Discussion failed to connect physiology and conservation') rather than on the authors' competence. Example revision shows removing 'the authors' and targeting the text. Avoid phrasing that attributes failure or intent to the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Write reviews without emotive, sarcastic, or needlessly negative tone; avoid communicating your emotional state or using language that demeans the work or authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove reviewer-oriented emotive phrases (e.g. 'I was disappointed') and replace with factual statements. Avoid subjective adjectives ('terrible', 'poorly'), depreciatory modifiers ('barely'), implicative verbs ('didn't manage to'), narration ('I didn't bother reading'), rhetorical questions ('are the authors aware of'), universalizing claims ('as is abundantly clear'), speculation ('I bet the authors don't'), and overly expressive punctuation ('This is wrong!'). Rephrase to factual, descriptive language (e.g. 'There was a lack of connection...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that your comments are subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and signpost that your interpretation is one reader's perspective and not an absolute fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preface subjective judgments with phrases like 'I felt that...' so authors understand the comment is interpretive. This provides a non-authoritative buffer and promotes collegiality; use when appropriate to indicate perception rather than objective error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add context to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why you see an issue and how it affects readers' interpretation, rather than just stating a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete context or examples showing how text is unclear or how a claim lacks support. For instance, explain how the Discussion highlights physiology but only implies conservation and why making the linkage explicit would help readers. Context helps authors identify and fix the perceived shortcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide directed and actionable ways for authors to address comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Give specific, practical suggestions for how authors could fix the problem you raise rather than leaving them to guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest concrete edits (e.g. 'add a paragraph explicitly highlighting how physiological knowledge will aid conservation'), indicate whether the suggestion is essential or optional, and if you cannot think of a fix, admit this rather than leaving vague criticism. Actionable advice aids revision and subsequent evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with the ethics of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should know and adhere to ethical standards governing peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult COPE's 'Ethical guidelines for peer reviewers' and journal-specific reviewer guidance. Treat ethical knowledge as essential, including conflict-of-interest disclosure, confidentiality, and proper use of editorial fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember peer review is not meant to crush souls
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that reviews affect authors' careers and mental health; maintain collegiality even while being critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver criticism thoughtfully and constructively without reducing standards. Ask whether your review will help develop the scientist and the paper or merely harm the author. Consider impacts on ECRs and underrepresented groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and check implicit biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively consider and minimise conscious and unconscious biases that could influence your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for biases related to authors' nationality/language, geography, gender, institution, career stage, perceived fame, or other attributes. Ensure recommendations (e.g. for English editing) are grounded in manuscript examples and not stereotypes. Use journal procedures (conflict declarations) and self-reflection to reduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the forest, not the trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise substantive scientific issues (concepts, methods, interpretation) over exhaustive lists of minor grammatical or typographic errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many small language errors exist, give a single comment noting numerous grammar issues, provide 2–3 examples, and recommend thorough editing (or copy-editing post-acceptance). Emphasise scientific content and methodological rigour in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write your review with proper etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose reviewer comments using clear, complete sentences and appropriate grammar and structure; avoid sloppy or hypocritical reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your review itself demonstrates the standards you expect: no incomplete sentences, no fragmented points. Hasty, poorly written reviews can be perceived as hypocritical and undermine collegiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that writing styles are diverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Different authors have different stylistic choices; do not insist authors rewrite in your personal style when the text already communicates effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend changes when a sentence fails to relay the intended message, but avoid requiring style alignment. When suggesting stylistic edits, explain the rationale and focus on clarity/readability rather than personal preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest references mindfully and provide full citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend additional literature cautiously, always as suggestions (not requirements), and include full bibliographic details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit suggested citations to unreferenced statements or new text you propose. Avoid coercive or excessive self-citation (citation manipulation). Provide complete citations so authors can access the work and judge its appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide positive comments when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance critique with recognition of well-executed parts of the manuscript to encourage authors and reinforce good practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include affirmative feedback on strengths, but avoid excessive emotive praise. Balanced comments increase authors' receptivity and support fair assessment; don't let praise obscure necessary critical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit your review on time, or request an extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet review deadlines or proactively communicate with editors if you cannot, and decline invitations if unable to review within the timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot meet a deadline, request more time or decline and suggest alternative reviewers. If you accept and then cannot complete, notify the editorial office. Timely reviews help editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider signing your reviews, if comfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to reveal your identity to authors, weighing transparency and recognition against potential power dynamics and risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing can incentivise collegial tone and provide credit, but can also create pressure, reduce critical candour, or enable coercive behaviour (e.g. attempting co-authorship). Only sign if comfortable and ensure it does not compromise impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'confidential comments to the editor' field appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use confidential editorial comments for information not suitable for authors (ethics concerns, conflicts, rationale for scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report suspected misconduct, conflicts of interest, or rationale for low scores in this field. Do not use it to vent frustrations unprofessionally. Provide support for scores when relevant and keep the same constructive standards as for author-facing comments.
